source: original questions written against the public CCAO-F blueprint (Exam Guide v1.0)

questions.stem: A product marketing manager asks Claude to "write a LinkedIn post about our new analytics tool." The draft is generic cheerleading with no product specifics and the wrong tone for the IT directors she is targeting, and the product briefing she is holding never entered the conversation. What is the most effective next step?
options: Ask Claude to make the post more engaging and professional without adding any new information.
Add the product briefing as source material and specify the audience (IT directors), the format (short post), and the tone, then ask Claude to rewrite.
Switch to the most capable model available and re-run the same request for higher quality.
Accept the draft and edit it into shape by hand, since editing is faster than re-prompting.
questions.why: — The generic output is a missing-input problem: the prompt never supplied the audience, source material, or format, so the model filled the gaps with its average. Asking for "more engaging" adds no new information, a stronger model executes the same under-specified request, and manual editing treats the symptom while the next request repeats it.

questions.stem: An HR business partner uploads thirty pages of policy documents and asks Claude for a complete new-hire onboarding curriculum with modules, exercises, and a quiz bank. The result is generic and drifts from the documents. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Repeat the request, adding that the curriculum must be "comprehensive, accurate, and based only on the attached documents."
Ask Claude to evaluate its own first draft against the documents and produce an improved full curriculum.
Sequence the work: have Claude extract and organize the key policies, review that extraction, approve a module outline, then draft each module against the verified outline.
Start a new chat and re-issue the original request to get a different attempt.
questions.why: — Decomposing the sprawling request into checked steps fixes the root cause: unverified source facts and an unreviewed structure. Re-asking with stronger adjectives changes emphasis, not structure; self-review uses the same process that produced the flaw; and a fresh chat re-rolls the same overloaded request from zero.

questions.stem: A consultant's client update comes back stiff and three times too long. She likes the content and wants to fix the draft without losing it. Which approach is most effective?
options: Open a new chat and try again with the same request, hoping for a better result.
Stay in the conversation and give specific direction: cut it to one page, open with the delay and its cost to the client, drop the methodology paragraph, and write for a busy CFO.
Ask Claude to rate its own draft out of ten and revise the sections that score low.
Ask Claude to "make it better and more professional" and accept whatever comes back.
questions.why: — A corrective follow-up is a new input: naming what to change and for whom narrows the space of acceptable outputs. A restart discards accumulated context and re-rolls the dice, self-scoring invites a polite yes, and "make it better" gives the model nothing new to act on.

questions.stem: A communications lead wants Claude to draft a weekly update email that sounds like the company's CEO, and several authentic past weekly emails from the CEO exist. Which approach is most effective?
options: Instruct Claude to "write in a confident, visionary, executive tone" and provide the weekly facts.
Ask Claude to study how well-known CEOs write weekly updates and imitate that style.
Add three of the CEO's past weekly emails to a Project with a short note on the recurring structure, then ask for this week's update from the bullet-point facts.
Describe the desired tone in detail - sentence length, vocabulary, rhythm - without providing any samples.
questions.why: — Real samples of the target voice are the only reliable style evidence, and a Project makes them reusable every week. Tone adjectives and tone specs describe style abstractly and still leave the model guessing what this CEO sounds like, and imitating famous CEOs imports someone else's voice entirely.

questions.stem: An analyst uploads a spreadsheet of regional sales figures and asks Claude to "find insights." Which approach is most effective?
options: Ask Claude first to summarize what the data contains and which questions it can actually answer, then run the analyses that matter and check the key figures against the spreadsheet before using them.
Ask Claude to find the most interesting and actionable insights in the data and highlight anything surprising.
Use the most capable model available so the analysis is as deep as possible, with the same one-line request.
Ask Claude to flag any errors or unsupported numbers in its own analysis before delivering it.
questions.why: — Analysis starts from what the data actually contains, so a structure-first pass plus human verification anchors the work in real numbers. "Find interesting insights" invites unsupported claims, a stronger model deepens a guessed direction without changing the missing specification, and self-flagging is not a reliable check.

questions.stem: A strategy associate needs a current, sourced picture of a fast-moving market segment, and the accuracy of the sources matters more than speed. Which approach best fits the task?
options: Ask the chat model to "be thorough and cite reliable sources" from its general knowledge.
Ask for a single confident recommendation and treat the most detailed answer as the most accurate.
Run the same chat request several times and keep the version that reads best.
Use research mode to gather breadth with citations, ask for sources, and spot-check the citations driving the conclusions.
questions.why: — Research is where confident fabrication does the most damage, so a sourced, cited approach with spot-checking fits time-sensitive research. Asking the model to cite from memory produces plausible-looking references, a detailed answer is not a verified one, and selecting between runs by feel chooses style over evidence.

questions.stem: A marketing lead needs a wide set of possible names for a new campaign and is deliberately open to unusual options before narrowing down. Which prompting approach best fits this task?
options: Ask for the single best name so the team is not overwhelmed by options.
Ask for ten safe, on-brand names to avoid wasting discussion time.
Ask Claude to research competitor campaign names and pick the strongest one.
Ask for a large quantity of options, including deliberately odd ones, then run a second pass to critique and shortlist.
questions.why: — Brainstorming wants quantity and permission to be strange; the first few ideas are the average ones, so a large set plus a critique pass fits the task. A single "best" answer, a small safe set, and research-and-pick all collapse the option space before the team can explore it.

questions.stem: A delivery lead needs a long client proposal drafted, and the firm has past proposals that show the house voice and structure. Which approach is most effective?
options: Ask for the finished proposal in one request and edit whatever comes back.
Describe the firm's tone in adjectives and ask for the complete document at once.
Ask Claude to write in a "high-quality consulting style" and trust the defaults to match the firm.
Supply the audience, purpose, and format up front, give past proposals as voice examples, and iterate section by section.
questions.why: — Drafting benefits from an explicit audience, examples of the target voice, and section-by-section iteration. A one-shot request for the whole document, tone adjectives without samples, and trusting generic defaults all substitute the model's average for the firm's actual house style.

questions.stem: A consultant asks Claude for a one-page industry briefing for a client. The draft includes a specific statistic attributed to a named research firm, and it ships tomorrow. What is the most appropriate action before sending it?
options: Send it as-is - Claude's drafts are generally reliable and the deadline is tomorrow.
Verify the statistic and its attribution against the named firm's actual published report before sending.
Ask Claude how confident it is in the statistic and send it if Claude says it is certain.
Reword the line to say the segment "grew significantly" so precision is no longer claimed.
questions.why: — A named attribution is exactly the kind of specific, checkable detail models fabricate, and a client-facing number needs validation against the source that owns the fact. Sending as-is stakes the relationship on an unverified number, self-reported confidence is not an accuracy signal, and softening the wording hides the risk instead of resolving it.

questions.stem: Claude drafts customer-segment profiles from your uploaded survey data. One profile makes broad generalizations about an age group's attitudes toward technology that the survey never asked about. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ship it - the profiles came from analysis of your uploaded data, so they reflect the data.
Ask Claude whether the profiles are biased and revise whatever Claude flags.
Keep the profile but add a disclaimer that the analysis is AI-generated and may contain bias.
Cut or rebase the unsupported generalizations on what the survey actually shows, and add a counter-framing pass to your review routine.
questions.why: — Unsupported generalizations about a demographic are the bias this domain expects you to catch, and the fix is rebasing on real data plus a deliberate counter-framing check. Shipping assumes provenance implies accuracy, self-audit relies on the process that produced the flaw, and a disclaimer ships the same content with a footer.

questions.stem: A project manager uses Claude's research mode to produce a vendor-comparison report for a leadership decision. The report is well-structured and every claim carries a citation. What is the most appropriate action before presenting it?
options: Spot-check the citations behind the decision-driving claims against the linked primary sources, and confirm the sources are current and credible.
Present it - research mode's citations mean the claims have already been verified.
Ask Claude to confirm that all citations are real and accurately reflect the sources.
Regenerate the report with different wording and present the version whose recommendation feels better supported.
questions.why: — A citation tells you where to look, not that the claim holds; diligence means reading the primary sources behind the decision. Presenting on citation presence trusts the format, asking Claude to confirm its own citations is the model checking itself, and choosing between drafts by feel selects style over evidence.

questions.stem: Claude drafts an internal FAQ explaining parental-leave entitlements, including jurisdiction-specific rules employees will rely on for personal decisions. What is the most appropriate action before publishing?
options: Publish it - parental-leave rules are standard HR topics that models handle reliably.
Send it to the HR compliance specialist with jurisdiction expertise for verification and sign-off before publishing.
Ask Claude to verify each jurisdiction's rules against the latest regulations and publish once Claude confirms.
Publish it with a note telling employees to verify their own entitlements with HR if in doubt.
questions.why: — Benefits information employees rely on is consequential, so a qualified human must verify and own it before publication. Topic familiarity is not accuracy, self-verification leaves the model grading its own homework, and a disclaimer transfers the organization's duty onto each employee.

questions.stem: A consultant has a verified, detailed vendor-analysis document. The client's non-technical board needs a short version to decide whether to renew a contract. What is the most appropriate way to produce it?
options: Send the full document - the board can focus on the parts they need and will appreciate the depth.
Ask Claude to make the document shorter and more engaging, then send whichever version reads better.
Extract the executive summary paragraph Claude wrote at the top of the document and send that alone.

Ask Claude to rewrite it for a non-technical board with ten minutes, keeping the key cost figures and the main risk finding exact, then compare the rewrite against the original to confirm the substance survived.
questions.why: — Adaptation needs an explicit audience brief - reader, decision, time, and the claims that must survive verbatim - plus a comparison so simplification does not change the substance. Sending the full document outsources the editing, "shorter and more engaging" yields polish without fit, and the auto-summary was never checked against the board's decision.

questions.stem: A team will weight and score several vendor options in a live working session, adjusting scores as they debate. The comparison currently exists as a wall of prose in a chat. What is the most appropriate format?
options: Leave it as prose - the narrative explains the trade-offs better than a table would.
Have Claude present the comparison as a structured table the team can sort, weight, and update.
Convert it to a polished one-page document artifact to present in the meeting.
Keep the prose but ask Claude to bold the key numbers so they stand out.
questions.why: — The output feeds a downstream process of sorting, weighting, and recalculation, so structured data is the format that fits. Prose cannot be scored in the room, a presentation artifact is for reading not computing, and bolding numbers leaves the underlying structure unusable.

questions.stem: A marketer asked Claude for a competitive overview of three rivals: founding year, headquarters, and pricing tiers. The draft is fluent, with specific dates and figures. Before it goes into a client deck, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Use it as-is - the level of specific detail suggests the model had good information.
Ask Claude to double-check its own facts and use the draft once it confirms them.
Treat the specific dates and figures as claims to verify against each rival's own published information before use.
Add a footnote that the figures are approximate so the deck is not overclaiming.
questions.why: — Fluent, specific detail is exactly what a fabrication looks like, so each concrete claim needs checking against the source that owns it. Specificity is not a reliability signal, self-checking uses the model as its own reference, and a footnote does not make an unverified number safe.

questions.stem: A long Claude-generated analysis reports 412 survey respondents in its summary paragraph, while a chart in the same output is built on 380 responses. What should the reviewer do?
options: Use the summary figure, since the prose is the primary content and charts are illustrative.
Reconcile the discrepancy against the source data before the analysis is used, since internal consistency is the reviewer's responsibility.
Ask Claude which number is correct and trust its answer.
Remove both numbers to avoid the inconsistency entirely.
questions.why: — A long output has no built-in cross-check, so the reviewer is the consistency contract and must reconcile the figures against the source. Choosing a number by format, asking the model to adjudicate, and deleting the numbers all avoid resolving which figure is actually right.

questions.stem: A manager uses Claude to draft internal guidance on notice periods and severance that will be given to employees in three states. The wording reads authoritative. What is the most appropriate action before it is shared?
options: Share it - the guidance is internal and clearly labeled as a draft.
Ask Claude to confirm the guidance reflects current law in all three states.
Add a line telling employees the guidance is not legal advice and distribute it.
Route it to employment counsel or the qualified HR/legal owner for review and sign-off before distribution.
questions.why: — Legal and benefits content employees rely on is consequential, so a qualified human must own it before distribution. Internal labeling does not reduce reliance, self-confirmation leaves the model assessing its own legal accuracy, and a disclaimer transfers risk without adding the required review.

questions.stem: A verified research summary is dense and thorough. A busy executive has asked for "just the headline and the one number that matters." Which action best fits the request?
options: Send the full summary so the executive has all the context.
Produce a short version with an explicit brief - one headline and the single decision-driving number - and confirm that number matches the verified source.
Ask Claude to shorten it and make it more engaging, then send the result.
Trim it by hand by deleting paragraphs until it feels about right.
questions.why: — The audience and their decision are the brief, and the number that drives the decision must survive unchanged, so a targeted short version with a substance check fits. Sending everything ignores the request, a blind shorten-and-engage changes emphasis without a brief, and trimming by feel can drop the very number that matters.

questions.stem: A support team wants a set of policy answers they will reuse, edit over time, and share with new hires. The answers currently live as chat messages that scroll away. What is the most appropriate format?
options: Leave them in the chat and search the conversation whenever an answer is needed.
Save the answers as an editable, shareable document artifact the team can revise and hand off.
Paste them into a spreadsheet so each answer is one cell.
Ask Claude to repeat the answers whenever a new hire needs them.
questions.why: — The output has a life beyond the chat - reused, edited, and shared - so an artifact is the container that fits. Scrollback loses the content, a spreadsheet misrepresents prose answers as data, and regenerating each time produces drift instead of a maintained reference.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude a quick conceptual question to unblock a task and only needs the answer in the moment to keep working. What is the most appropriate format?
options: Turn the answer into a document artifact so it is preserved.
Ask for a structured table so the answer is well organized.
Request a formal report so the reasoning is fully documented.
Keep the answer inline in the conversation, since it is consumed now and not reused.
questions.why: — Format follows downstream use: an answer consumed immediately belongs inline. An artifact, a table, or a formal report adds overhead for content that will not be reused, edited, or processed.

questions.stem: A Claude-generated market summary presents only evidence that supports one conclusion and omits a well-known counterargument that appears in the source material. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Use it - a clear, single conclusion is more persuasive for the audience.
Recognize the one-sided framing as bias, add the omitted counter-evidence from the source, and rebalance the summary before use.
Ask Claude whether the summary is one-sided and fix whatever it flags.
Add a disclaimer that the summary may not reflect all viewpoints.
questions.why: — One-sided framing that omits contrary evidence is bias, and the repair is rebasing the summary on what the source actually contains. A single conclusion that hides contrary evidence misleads, self-audit relies on the process that produced the framing, and a disclaimer ships the same imbalance.

questions.stem: A consultant runs daily conversations about the same client, re-pasting the same brand guidelines and campaign notes into a new chat every morning and scrolling back to find the latest approved draft every afternoon. Which choice best fits the workflow?
options: Keep using new chats but enable research mode each morning so Claude re-reads the pasted material more thoroughly.
Create a Project for the client with the guidelines and notes as project knowledge, and develop drafts as artifacts within it.
Switch to the most capable model so it retains the guidelines better across separate chats.
Email the guidelines each morning and continue drafting in a regular chat.
questions.why: — Recurring context belongs in a Project and a revisable deliverable belongs in an artifact, so both recurring costs disappear. Research mode adds breadth she never asked for and still requires pasting, a stronger model does not carry memory across chats, and emailing adds a manual step without fixing anything.

questions.stem: An associate must generate a high volume of short customer-reply drafts where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning. Which choice best fits the task?
options: Use the most capable model so every draft meets the highest quality bar regardless of cost.
Draft in bulk with whatever model is default, then rerun every draft through the most capable model for polish.
Use the fast, low-cost model tier, reserving the most capable model for the complex or sensitive cases that need it.
Switch to a different platform known for cheaper generation.
questions.why: — Aligning model selection with task requirements means matching a faster, lower-cost tier to straightforward, high-volume work. Always using the top model wastes the cost and latency budget, a double pass through the top model doubles both for no gain, and switching platforms abandons a workable answer to a trade-off that exists everywhere.

questions.stem: A PM must summarize forty internal team emails into a daily digest by 9 a.m. and separately produce a client-facing strategy narrative that anchors a seven-figure renewal. Both are due tomorrow. Which approach best fits the tasks?
options: Draft the internal digest with the fast, low-cost tier and develop the client-facing narrative with the most capable model.
Run both tasks through the most capable model so nothing ships below the highest quality bar.
Run both through the fast tier to protect the deadline, then improve the narrative manually if time allows.
Postpone the digest and use research mode to gather supporting sources for the narrative first.
questions.why: — The two tasks name opposite constraints, so they get opposite tiers: high-volume internal work optimizes speed and cost while the high-stakes deliverable spends capability. Running both on the top model wastes budget, running both on the fast tier risks the renewal narrative, and research mode lets the required digest slip.

questions.stem: A week-long working thread has accumulated research notes, abandoned drafts, and side questions. Claude now contradicts early instructions and revives discarded ideas, but the analysis must continue with the agreed constraints. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Switch to the most capable model in the same thread so Claude can hold the full history more reliably.
Ask Claude to summarize the current state - decisions, constraints, next steps - then continue in a fresh chat from that summary.
Keep working in the same thread and paste the original instructions at the bottom of each new message.
Start a completely fresh chat with no summary, restating the task from memory.
questions.why: — When the work must continue, summarizing compresses what matters and a fresh chat restores usable context. A model upgrade does not recover instructions crowded out of a full context, re-pasting into the same thread adds load to the overload, and a bare restart discards the decisions the continuation depends on.

questions.stem: A long conversation produced a completed market analysis. The associate now needs to start an unrelated piece of work, and nothing from the old thread is relevant to it. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue in the same thread so all the work stays in one place.
Switch to a more capable model in the existing thread to handle the new task.
Start a fresh chat for the new task, since the old context has served its purpose and would only add noise.
Paste the entire old thread into a new chat so nothing is lost.
questions.why: — Restart is the right memory move when the task has changed and the old context is no longer relevant, because carrying it forward only adds load. Continuing in the same thread drags in stale context, a model upgrade does not help, and pasting the whole thread into a new chat imports the same noise.

questions.stem: A team re-establishes the same style guide and audience rules at the start of every new conversation, and quality varies with whoever remembers to include them. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask each team member to keep a personal checklist of the rules to paste in.
Use the most capable model so it applies the rules more consistently from the conversation.
Persist the style guide and audience rules as Project instructions and knowledge so every conversation inherits them.
Add the rules as a one-time note at the end of each finished conversation.
questions.why: — Context that recurs across sessions belongs in a Project so no conversation has to re-establish it. Personal checklists depend on memory, a stronger model does not persist instructions across chats, and adding rules after the work is done changes nothing.

questions.stem: An analyst needs a broad, current survey of an emerging topic with traceable sources, and is willing to wait longer for it. Which Claude surface best fits the task?
options: Use research mode, which searches extensively and returns cited findings.
Use a single chat answer drawn from the model's general knowledge for speed.
Create a Project and upload old articles so the answer is grounded.
Ask the fast, low-cost tier for a quick overview and accept the result.
questions.why: — The task demands sourced breadth, which is exactly what research mode provides, at the cost of time and usage. A general-knowledge chat answer lacks sourcing, a Project only grounds the model in whatever old material is uploaded, and the fast tier trades away the depth the task requires.

questions.stem: A team lead receives an unstructured complaint email about a slow internal approval process and needs a shared understanding of the requirements before proposing changes. Which approach is most effective?
options: Ask Claude to read the email and produce a recommended process redesign for the team to vote on.
Forward the email to the process owner and let them decide what the complaint means without analysis.
Have Claude conduct a full requirements analysis, sign off on the requirements, and present them as final.
Ask Claude to extract the stated needs, unstated assumptions, constraints, and open questions as separate lists, then review the lists with the process owner to confirm which requirements are real.
questions.why: — Claude adds the most value structuring unstructured input into needs, assumptions, constraints, and questions, with the human owner validating the result. Redesigning straight from one email skips the requirements step, forwarding with no analysis wastes the tool, and letting Claude sign off hands a judgment call to a tool with no authority.

questions.stem: A PM needs a project plan by the end of the week and has forty pages of process notes, post-mortems, and wiki pages to build it from. Which approach is most effective?
options: Ask Claude to research the notes and produce the final plan, then circulate it so work can begin immediately.
Write the plan entirely by hand from the notes, since planning accountability cannot be shared with a tool.
Ask Claude to synthesize the source material into a working picture and draft two or three plan approaches with pros and cons, then verify key claims and add stakeholder judgment before finalizing.
Assign the plan to a rotating committee so no single person bears the research workload.
questions.why: — Claude compresses synthesis and drafting while the human verifies claims and adds judgment the notes do not contain. Forwarding Claude's plan as final skips verification, writing by hand rejects the leverage, and a committee adds coordination cost without changing how the research gets done.

questions.stem: A team has three candidate process designs for a loan-intake redesign and a client review on Monday. Which approach is most effective for using Claude to support design and iteration?
options: Give Claude the agreed requirements and ask it to critique each candidate against them, then draft variations; the team reviews the critiques and selects the design with the client.
Ask Claude to pick the best of the three designs and present that one to keep the review focused.
Ask Claude to produce a brand-new design from scratch so the team can compare a fourth option.
Keep Claude out of the design phase and use it only to document the approved design afterward.
questions.why: — Critiquing each candidate against the requirements and drafting variations is the iteration support that hardens a design, with the team keeping selection authority. Letting Claude pick hands design authority to a tool with no accountability, generating from scratch discards the team's work, and restricting Claude to documentation wastes it where critique adds the most value.

questions.stem: An HR team's hiring workflow has six steps: screen resumes, run a phone screen, write the hiring-manager summary, schedule interviews, run the interview, and make the hiring decision. The HR lead wants to integrate Claude. Which approach is most effective?
options: Have Claude draft the resume-screening notes and hiring-manager summaries, keep the interview and hiring decision human, and have recruiters make shortlist calls using Claude's screening notes.
Delegate the entire screening-and-decision pipeline to Claude so recruiters can focus on closing candidates.
Keep the entire workflow human and use Claude only to answer general hiring-best-practice questions.
Insert a mandatory committee review between Claude and every downstream step of the workflow.
questions.why: — Sorting steps individually puts pattern-based drafting with Claude, keeps judgment and accountability steps human, and uses Claude's output where a human still decides. Delegating the whole pipeline hands over irreversible decisions, keeping everything manual rejects the leverage, and a review on every step adds cost uniformly instead of matching oversight to risk.

questions.stem: A stakeholder deciding whether to approve a Claude-assisted document-intake workflow asks what benefits it will deliver and what its limitations are. Which response is most effective?
options: Explain that drafting and summarization will drop from hours to minutes with human review of every output, while noting Claude can present incorrect information confidently and must not make final approval decisions.
Emphasize that Claude will fully automate the intake process with guaranteed accuracy, since accuracy concerns can be addressed during rollout.
Describe Claude as an experimental chatbot with limited practical value so expectations stay low.
Decline to characterize Claude's capabilities and recommend a multi-month governance review before discussing benefits.
questions.why: — A specific, calibrated answer - concrete time savings, human review checkpoints, and honest naming of hallucination risk - lets the stakeholder decide soundly. Promising full automation oversells, calling it a limited chatbot undersells real value, and deferring to a governance review leaves the stakeholder without the information the decision needs.

questions.stem: Before a planning kickoff, a delivery lead has a dozen past project post-mortems scattered across folders and wants a working picture of recurring failure themes. Which use of Claude fits best?
options: Have Claude summarize and cluster the post-mortems into recurring themes and open questions for the team to review.
Have Claude pick the single most important lesson and set the project's priorities around it.
Skip the synthesis and start planning, since post-mortems are historical and not directly relevant.
Ask Claude to predict which failures this project will hit and plan around the predictions.
questions.why: — Claude is strongest at converting scattered material into an organized working picture before planning starts. Picking one lesson collapses the evidence, skipping synthesis discards the input, and asking for predictions treats the model's speculation as researched fact.

questions.stem: A manager must present three possible sequencing approaches for a rollout to a sponsor who will choose one. Which approach is most effective?
options: Ask Claude to draft each approach with its pros, cons, and underlying assumptions, then verify the key claims and add the political and stakeholder judgment the notes lack.
Ask Claude to choose the best approach and present that single recommendation.
Present only the approach the manager already favors, using Claude to write it up.
Have Claude rank the approaches by a score it assigns and present the ranking.
questions.why: — Claude expands the option set with pros, cons, and assumptions, while the human verifies claims and adds judgment the source material does not contain. A single recommendation, a write-up of a predetermined choice, and a self-assigned score all hand the sponsor a decision stripped of the comparison and judgment they need.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to handle a new step in an existing workflow, but that step produces a recommendation that will be forwarded to a regulator. Which approach is most effective?
options: Automate the step end-to-end since the workflow already has other automated steps.
Skip the step entirely because the output touches a regulator.
Use Claude to draft the recommendation with the supporting analysis, and require a qualified human to review, adjust, and own the version that is forwarded.
Add a disclaimer to the forwarded recommendation noting it was AI-assisted.
questions.why: — Integrating Claude into a workflow means sorting steps by risk: Claude drafts the information-heavy work while a qualified human owns the consequential, externally facing output. Full automation removes the accountability the regulator requires, skipping the step discards the leverage, and a disclaimer does not add the required human owner.

questions.stem: A recruiter wants to speed up shortlisting. Claude can draft screening notes from resumes, but the shortlist decision is the recruiter's. Which division of labor fits best?
options: Claude ranks all candidates and the recruiter forwards the top slice unchanged.
Claude drafts the screening notes and the recruiter reviews them and makes the shortlist decision.
The recruiter screens every resume by hand and uses Claude only to format the final list.
Claude makes the shortlist and the recruiter reviews it only if a candidate complains.
questions.why: — This is the Claude-assisted human bucket: the human decides with Claude's prep in front of them. Forwarding a machine ranking unchanged delegates the decision, screening everything by hand discards the drafting leverage, and reviewing only on complaint removes the human from the routine decision.

questions.stem: An operations lead is pitching a Claude-assisted workflow to a skeptical team and must describe what will and will not change. Which framing is most effective?
options: Name the specific steps Claude will draft, the review checkpoints that stay human, and the known limitations, with both benefits and limitations stated concretely.
Promise full automation to show the team the biggest possible upside.
Downplay the tool as "just a drafting aid" so the team is not threatened.
Avoid specifics and let the pilot results speak for themselves later.
questions.why: — Communicating value and limitations means calibrated specifics in both directions, so the team can trust the change. Overselling breaks trust at the first failure, underselling blocks a justified pilot, and avoiding specifics leaves the team without the honest picture adoption depends on.

questions.stem: A marketing associate pastes the same brand guidelines and audience notes into every new Claude conversation, and outputs drift whenever she forgets. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Save the guidelines in a text file on her desktop so she can paste them faster each morning.
Keep pasting as before but add a calendar reminder to check every chat for missing context.
Create a Claude Project with the brand guidelines and audience notes as custom instructions and knowledge, and start all marketing conversations inside it.
Ask Claude to remember the guidelines from earlier conversations and apply them automatically.
questions.why: — A Project makes the context structural so every conversation inherits the instructions and knowledge. A faster paste still fails the day it is skipped, a reminder manages the symptom, and chats do not carry reliable memory across conversations - that persistence is what Projects provide.

questions.stem: A sales Project was given an uploaded copy of the pricing sheet. Finance now revises prices in Google Drive every month, and Claude keeps quoting last month's numbers. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Connect the Project to Google Drive so it references the pricing sheet at its source, and remove the stale uploaded copy.
Keep the uploaded file but add a note telling Claude prices may be outdated and to hedge its answers.
Re-upload the current pricing sheet at the start of every week so the copy is fresh.
Instruct the sales team to verify every price Claude quotes against the Drive file before sending anything.
questions.why: — A connector makes currency structural and removing the stale upload eliminates the competing copy. Hedging teaches vagueness instead of correctness, weekly re-uploads are a manual sync loop that fails the week it is skipped, and pushing verification onto every user pays the staleness tax forever.

questions.stem: A consulting Project's custom instructions say "write professionally and be helpful." Every session the team re-explains that client updates must be five-section memos in plain language for a non-technical steering committee. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Rewrite the Project's custom instructions to state the requirements concretely: audience, five-section structure, plain-language rule, and which knowledge file is authoritative.
Ask Claude at the start of each session to remember the memo format from the previous conversation.
Expand the custom instructions to "you are a world-class consultant who always produces flawless, professional work."
Paste an example memo into each conversation whenever the format comes out wrong.
questions.why: — The format rule is standing policy, so it belongs as concrete, enforceable custom instructions the Project applies every time. Relying on cross-chat memory, flattering adjectives, and per-conversation examples all re-supply context the configuration should already carry.

questions.stem: A company extended its returns window from 30 to 60 days and dropped a fee in July. The support Project still holds the January policy file, and an associate has been correcting the window in each draft reply for two weeks. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep correcting the window manually in each reply, since the associate is already fast at it.
Update the Project: replace the outdated returns policy file with the current one and review the custom instructions for anything else the change affects.
Add an instruction telling Claude that return-window answers may have changed and to be less certain.
Tell the support team to rely on the Project only for drafting tone and verify every policy detail on the intranet.
questions.why: — The stale file is the root cause, so replacing it fixes every future conversation at once. Manual correction leaves the wrong source producing the next wrong draft, hedging makes Claude vague instead of correct, and routing humans to the intranet abandons the Project when a one-time update restores it.

questions.stem: A team is setting up a Project. One knowledge source is a finalized company policy manual that changes about once a year; another is a shared document that the marketing team edits weekly. How should each be configured?
options: Upload both as knowledge files and re-upload them whenever anyone remembers.
Connect both sources so neither requires manual refreshing.
Upload both as knowledge files and add an instruction to always use the latest version.
Upload the stable policy manual as a knowledge file and connect the frequently edited document at its source.
questions.why: — The deciding factor is how often the underlying material changes: stable, finished reference belongs as an upload, and living documents that change on a schedule belong behind a connector. Re-uploading by hand is a sync loop, connecting the yearly manual adds complexity the upload does not need, and an instruction cannot make a stale upload current.

questions.stem: A Project holds two files that disagree on the current escalation procedure, and Claude keeps citing the superseded one. Which configuration change best addresses this?
options: Remove the superseded file and state in the Project instructions which document is authoritative.
Add an instruction telling Claude to prefer the newer-sounding document when files disagree.
Upload a third file summarizing the difference and let Claude choose.
Leave both files and ask the team to specify the right procedure in each conversation.
questions.why: — A Project that holds competing versions has no way to know which wins, so removing the stale file and naming the authoritative source in the instructions fixes it. Guessing by filename, adding a third file, and re-specifying in every conversation all leave the conflict in place.

questions.stem: A support Project's knowledge and instructions were set up eight months ago and have not been touched since, though the company has changed several processes. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave the configuration as-is, since it worked when it was set up.
Wait until a customer notices a wrong answer before changing anything.
Rebuild the Project from scratch every quarter regardless of what changed.
Review the Project's instructions and knowledge sources on a schedule tied to how fast the underlying material changes, and update them as reality moves.
questions.why: — A configuration is correct as of a date, so maintenance means reviewing instructions and sources on a schedule and updating them when reality moves. Set-and-forget is the failure mode, waiting for a customer to catch an error is reactive, and rebuilding on a fixed calendar wastes effort when nothing relevant changed.

questions.stem: A procurement lead is short on time and proposes having Claude rank three vendors on a $2M contract and posting the ranking directly to the selection record with no human pass. Which use of Claude is most appropriate?
options: Let Claude produce and post the final ranking, since the proposals are non-confidential and the criteria are objective.
Let Claude post the ranking with a note that it was machine-generated so reviewers know no human judgment was involved.
Have Claude draft a structured comparison of the proposals, then the procurement lead reviews the draft, adjusts it, and signs the final recommendation.
Do not use Claude for any part of the vendor selection because the contract value is high.
questions.why: — Drafting the comparison keeps a qualified human as the decision-owner while Claude does the heavy lifting. Posting the ranking unreviewed hands a consequential decision to a model with no accountability, a disclaimer documents the gap instead of closing it, and refusing Claude entirely discards assistance the accountability test would allow.

questions.stem: A team lead proposes four uses of Claude for the coming quarter. Which one is inappropriate?
options: Claude drafts interview questions, and HR screens and rewrites them before any interviewer sees them.
Claude generates a first draft of a performance-improvement plan, and the manager edits, personalizes, and signs it.
Claude scores employees on layoff risk from their review files, and the ranked list goes to HR for termination planning with no human review of the scores.
Claude summarizes newly published industry regulations from public sources for the whole team.
questions.why: — The layoff scoring turns unreviewed model output into a consequential decision about people's jobs with no human accountable for the ranking. The other three keep a human in the loop, involve no decision about an individual, or touch neither personal data nor decisions about people.

questions.stem: An HR analyst wants Claude to summarize exit-interview transcripts that contain employee names and details about medical leave. Organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data outside approved systems. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Upload the transcripts as-is because they are internal HR documents and the summary is for internal use only.
Upload the transcripts with an instruction that Claude must not retain or remember any personal details.
Remove employee names and medical details from the transcripts, replacing them with role and department labels, then ask Claude to summarize the anonymized text.
Cancel the summarization and have the analyst read every transcript manually, since the data cannot leave the HR system.
questions.why: — Redacting names and medical details before upload lets the theme analysis proceed without exposing regulated data. Uploading as-is violates policy, a non-retention instruction is not a policy control because the data still leaves approved systems, and manual reading is unnecessary once anonymization enables the summary.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to upload a spreadsheet of customer names and account numbers so Claude can spot churn trends. Policy restricts sharing regulated personal data with third-party services. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Upload the spreadsheet as-is, since the analysis is internal and the data will not be shared further.
Upload it with an instruction telling Claude to ignore the personal fields during analysis.
Abandon the trend analysis because the data is regulated and cannot be used with Claude.
Replace names and account numbers with anonymous labels, then upload the anonymized data for the trend analysis.
questions.why: — Applying data-sensitivity safeguards means redacting or anonymizing regulated identifiers before use, so the analysis proceeds without exposing protected data. Uploading as-is violates policy, an instruction does not change what data left the systems, and abandoning the task is unnecessary when anonymization enables it.

questions.stem: The enterprise AI platform requires a 24-hour wait for new project access. A client deliverable is due tomorrow morning, and a teammate offers their personal Claude account for the client's confidential strategy documents. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Request expedited access through the approved process, and if it cannot be shortened, tell the client the timeline slipped rather than move their documents to an unapproved account.
Use the teammate's personal account tonight and delete the chat history afterward.
Upload the documents to the personal account but instruct Claude to treat everything as strictly confidential.
Proceed with the personal account tonight and disclose it to the manager tomorrow so the use is on record.
questions.why: — Keeping client data inside the approved platform preserves its handling agreements and audit trail, and an honest timeline conversation is a legitimate outcome. A personal account breaks the control set even with deleted history, a confidentiality instruction does not substitute for contractual protections, and disclosing afterward records a violation rather than preventing one.

questions.stem: A company's internal AI policy permits uploading business documents to the approved workspace, but a client's contract includes stricter confidentiality terms. A consultant plans to paste the client's confidential documents into the approved workspace. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Check the client contract's confidentiality terms first and follow whichever is stricter before the material touches any AI tool.
Proceed, since the internal policy already permits uploading business documents to the approved workspace.
Proceed with the approved workspace but delete the conversation afterward to protect the client.
Ask a teammate whether the client would mind, and proceed if they say it is probably fine.
questions.why: — Client and vendor contracts can be stricter than internal policy, so the stricter term governs and must be checked before the material is used. Internal policy is a floor not a ceiling, deletion does not satisfy confidentiality terms, and a teammate's informal assurance is not the authority for a contractual question.

questions.stem: A manager wants to use a new AI feature for customer data, and the organization's AI policy does not address that feature. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Proceed, since the policy does not explicitly prohibit the feature.
Proceed cautiously and stop only if a problem arises later.
Escalate the question to governance, legal, or the manager's own chain of authority rather than guessing.
Ask Claude whether the use is compliant and proceed if Claude says it is.
questions.why: — When policy is silent, the professional move is to escalate to the authority that owns the decision. Silence is not permission, acting-and-watching risks the exposure, and asking the model to assess its own compliance is not a governance control.

questions.stem: A marketing team used Claude to generate customer personas for a lending product's outreach campaign. The personas skew toward a single demographic, and the team plans to use them to prioritize outreach without further review. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Launch with the personas as-is, since Claude derived them from real market data that cannot be biased.
Prompt Claude to remove all bias from the personas and launch once the model confirms they are balanced.
Have the team review the personas for bias with diverse input, correct or regenerate them, and document that AI was used before the campaign proceeds.
Stop using AI for persona work entirely, since lending outreach can influence financial decisions.
questions.why: — A human bias review with correction and documentation keeps the campaign fair and accountable. Launching unreviewed lets inherited skew shape who hears about a lending product, asking the model to audit its own output adds no independent check, and banning AI personas discards useful assistance a review step makes safe.

questions.stem: A team used Claude to draft customer-facing campaign copy and a summary of customer issues that will shape how customers are treated next quarter. Which handling is most appropriate?
options: Publish without mentioning the AI's role, since the copy passed a read-through by the team.
Publish the copy but keep the AI's role confidential to avoid undermining confidence.
Discard the AI-generated content and produce everything manually to avoid any ethical concern.
Follow the organization's disclosure norms for the AI-generated material, verify the content, and keep a human accountable for the final output.
questions.why: — Ethical use means disclosing AI's role where it matters, verifying before shipping, and keeping a person answerable for effects on people. A read-through is not verification, hiding the AI's role conflicts with disclosure norms, and discarding useful content overshoots when verification and disclosure make it safe.

questions.stem: An associate's weekly report prompt produced focused one-page summaries for months. This week the output is generic and drops the section managers rely on most. The prompt text is unchanged, but the report it summarizes was reorganized into a new layout last week. What is the best first step?
options: Rewrite the entire prompt from scratch with different wording.
Compare a last good output with this week's, identify that the reorganized source layout is the cause, and update the prompt to point at the new layout.
Switch to a more capable model tier to raise output quality.
Send each week's generic output to a human reviewer to fix manually before it goes out.
questions.why: — The output changed exactly when the source's structure changed, so the root cause is the mismatch between the prompt and the reorganized report; comparing the last good output isolates that and updating the prompt fixes it. A rewrite discards working instructions, a model switch spends cost on a problem the model did not cause, and routing every output through a reviewer pays for the failure forever.

questions.stem: A marketing associate uses one prompt that asks Claude to research competitors, outline a positioning document, draft the full document, format it to the team template, and verify every claim. The output is long and the middle sections are consistently weak. Which approach is most likely to improve quality?
options: Add stronger wording to the single prompt demanding high quality and thoroughness across all five tasks.
Switch to the most capable model tier and keep the five-task prompt unchanged.
Run the same prompt twice and manually combine the strongest sections from both outputs.
Split the work into separate steps - research, outline, draft, format, verify - reviewing each step's output before moving to the next.
questions.why: — The middle sections are weak because five jobs are competing inside one response, so splitting into reviewed steps removes the competition. Demanding higher quality asks one response to do more at once, a more capable model raises the ceiling but leaves the overload, and running twice pays double for manual patchwork that still leaves the structure failing.

questions.stem: A sales team gives feedback that Claude's weekly product-update drafts are too technical for their customer audience. The drafts are generated by a saved prompt in the team's project. What is the best response to this feedback?
options: Manually simplify this week's draft before sending it to the team.
Ask each salesperson to rewrite their own portion of the update before it goes out.
Switch to a faster model tier so drafts arrive earlier and the team has more time to edit them.
Update the saved prompt and the project's instructions to specify the customer audience and plain language, then regenerate the next draft with the updated prompt.
questions.why: — The feedback points at the saved prompt's missing audience definition, so updating the standing prompt applies the fix to every future draft, and regenerating confirms it. Manually simplifying only this week's draft, spreading rework across salespeople, and a faster model all leave the cause in place.

questions.stem: A support team's project includes an uploaded product-pricing document from last year. Claude's answers keep quoting the old prices, and team members have been correcting each answer by hand before it reaches customers. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add an instruction to the prompt telling Claude to only provide current, accurate pricing information.
Have a human review and correct every pricing answer before it is sent.
Replace the outdated pricing document in the project's knowledge source with the current one, so every future answer draws on current data.
Move pricing questions to a more capable model tier.
questions.why: — Claude can only answer from the material it is given, so the year-old document is the root cause and replacing it fixes every future answer. An instruction to be accurate cannot create pricing the project does not contain, reviewing every answer pays the correction cost forever, and a more capable model still reads the same stale document.

questions.stem: A team's research workflow sends every question - including one-paragraph quick checks - through the same heavyweight path: a deep-dive request to the most capable model with a ten-section analysis format. Costs and turnaround keep climbing, and half the sections go unread. What is the most effective change?
options: Add a mandatory review step to every response so quality is protected across the workflow.
Switch the whole workflow to a different AI platform with lower pricing.
Add an instruction to the deep-dive prompt telling the model to keep answers short.
Route quick questions through a short prompt on a fast model and reserve the deep treatment for genuinely complex analysis.
questions.why: — Most workflow cost is structural: a mismatch between the task and the treatment, so matching the approach to the job removes it. A blanket review adds cost uniformly, switching platforms moves the same mismatch, and an instruction inside the heavyweight prompt does not change the path quick questions take.

questions.stem: A weekly report workflow outputs a fixed twelve-section format, but the audience only ever reads the summary and the two risk sections; the rest is never opened. The team wants to optimize for efficiency and effectiveness. What is the most appropriate change?
options: Keep all twelve sections so no potentially useful information is ever dropped.
Redesign the output to the sections the audience actually reads, and confirm after the change that the report still serves their needs.
Switch to the most capable model so the unread sections are at least higher quality.
Add an instruction asking the model to make the unread sections more engaging.
questions.why: — Optimization means auditing the moving parts and cutting what nobody uses, then measuring that the result still fits. Keeping unused sections preserves waste, a stronger model does not make unread content read, and making unread sections engaging does not remove the mismatch between the format and the audience.
